The answer 0 is incorrect, because the solution's claim that the coefficients must tend to 0 because the radius of convergence is 1 is false. A power series with radius of convergence 1 can have coefficients that do not decay. For example, 1/(1−x) has every coefficient equal to 1.

**Correct computation.** Let g(x) = (2025+x) ln(2025+x). It is analytic for |x| < 2025, so its Taylor coefficients a_k decay geometrically.

Partial fractions give

1/((x−1)(x−2)(x−3)) = −(1/2)·1/(1−x) + (1/2)·1/(1−x/2) − (1/6)·1/(1−x/3).

The coefficient of x^m in this expansion is c_m = −1/2 + (1/2)(1/2)^m − (1/6)(1/3)^m.

Then d_n = Σ_{k=0}^n a_k c_{n−k}. As n → ∞, the terms with (1/2)^m and (1/3)^m vanish, since the a_k decay fast. What remains is

lim d_n = −(1/2) Σ a_k = −(1/2) g(1) = −(1/2)(2026 ln 2026) = −1013 ln 2026.

This is nonzero, so the proposed answer 0 is wrong.

VERDICT: REJECT
